cards.title: Offer vs. discount: test structure, not depth
cards.summary: An offer is a stack of benefits and terms; swapping 10/20/30% off is only discount testing and rarely breaks a revenue ceiling.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to test next on your store's acquisition offer when discount-depth tests keep producing flat or temporary lifts.
steps: Define the offer as the full set of advantages a buyer gets: price, gift, credit, subscription terms, guarantee, access, exclusivity. A discount is only one component.
When planning a test, change the structure (subscription vs one-time, gift present vs absent, credit vs cash off) rather than only the percentage.
Put paid ad money and creative behind the testing so traffic is comparable across variants.

Example from the source: a CPG brand replaced a plain '20% off if you subscribe' with subscribe and get $10 off + three free gifts + a $20 future-credit gift card; the source reports lower CAC and higher repeat rates. Treat the specific result as their example, not a benchmark.
Keep the store's normal-price path visible as the comparison anchor so the offer reads as a stack, not a permanent markdown.
caveats: The presenter's brand results are case examples from his client work, not guaranteed outcomes.
The source states discount-only testing is the main reason brands stall; this is his opinion and does not cover price-elasticity or margin-constrained categories.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Front-loaded subscription discount formula
cards.summary: Give a large first-order discount and a small recurring one, because a flat recurring discount doesn't create urgency to subscribe now.
cards.use_when: Designing or reworking subscribe-and-save terms for a consumable product to lift first-order subscription opt-ins without permanently thinning margin.
steps: Stop relying on 'subscribe and save 15% every order' as the whole offer; the source argues it gives no reason to subscribe today.
Front-load: put the heavy discount on the first order (source examples: 25-30% off first order) and drop the recurring discount to roughly 5-10%.
Make the front-loaded benefit only available on subscription, and price one-time purchase higher.
Keep the recurring rate visible so the customer still sees a reason to stay subscribed.
Expect the margin effect to net out over the subscription life, and validate with 90-day LTV, not first-order margin alone.
caveats: The 25-30% first-order / 5-10% recurring numbers are the source's recommended range and cited brand examples (e.g. Armra), not tested universal thresholds.
The source states only about 10% of one-time buyers later subscribe, which is his claim; verify against your own cohort data.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Strategic welcome kit gifts that improve product use
cards.summary: Free gifts should help the customer consume the core product better, not be unrelated branded swag.
cards.use_when: Selecting the free gift or welcome-kit contents for a subscription or first-order offer on a consumable product.
steps: List what actually blocks or degrades the customer's experience of using your product (e.g., clumping, missing tool, wrong prep method).
Choose gifts that remove that block: the source's coffee example uses a creamer, an electric frother, a metal spoon, and a breathwork app.
Assign each gift a stated dollar value and display it in the offer so the stack looks larger than the discount alone.
Avoid tote bags and unrelated swag; the source says these add no consumption value and no retention.
Test gift combinations the same way you test discounts, and track whether gift recipients repeat at a higher rate.
caveats: Gift choices must fit your product; the coffee example is illustrative, not a template for every category.
The source also routes unit economics and sourcing of kit items to a separate discipline; do the COGS math before committing.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Four subscription offer models, ranked
cards.summary: From flat recurring discount to discount-plus-welcome-kit to subscription-only, the source ranks kit-based stacked offers as the strongest.
cards.use_when: Choosing which subscription offer architecture to run for a given brand and customer.
steps: Model 1 – basic recurring discount: 10-20% off every purchase, no gifts or front-loading. Lowest lift.
Model 2 – heavy front-loaded discount: e.g. 30% off first order, 5% recurring.
Model 3 – welcome kit: discount on recurring orders plus free gifts that support the product experience. Source calls this the strongest.
Model 4 – subscription only: no one-time purchase option at all; the customer must subscribe.
Pick based on category norms and test the price points, gifts, and terms rather than assuming one model is universal.
If you can't make a one-time and subscription path both profitable, model 4 removes the cheap alternative entirely.
caveats: The ranking is the presenter's opinion drawn from his client portfolio; it does not account for categories where one-time purchase is the norm.
Forcing subscription-only can suppress trial in high-consideration or high-price categories.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Raise list price, then discount to target
cards.summary: Fund a rich stacked offer by pricing higher and discounting down, so the visible discount is large relative to a high anchor.
cards.use_when: Structuring pricing and discount depth together so a stacked offer (gifts, credit, deep first-order discount) still protects net revenue.
steps: Set a higher list/one-time price as the anchor and compare the subscription or bundle price against it.
Apply the front-loaded discount to reach your intended net price for the first order.
Show the anchor price alongside the offer price so the savings are explicit (the source highlights how IM8 and AG1 show one-time vs subscription pricing side by side).
Check that the anchor is credible for your category so the discount doesn't read as fake.
Recheck margin at the net price, not the list price, including the cost of any gifts.
caveats: The source presents this as a common tactic among nine-figure brands; it says nothing about how consumers react to habitual fake anchors, and this can attract regulatory scrutiny in some markets.
Verify compliance with local pricing-display rules before running permanent anchor pricing.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Middle-option anchoring on bundles
cards.summary: Auto-select the middle bundle and price it against the single-unit price so the bundle becomes the default baseline.
cards.use_when: Designing bundle tiers and default selection on a PDP or bundle landing page for apparel, accessories, or repeat-purchase goods.
steps: Show the single unit price as the highest per-item price so every bundle reads as a saving.
Show three tiers (e.g., 1-pack, 3-pack, 6-pack) with the middle tier pre-selected and presented as the standard.
State the per-item price and total savings next to each tier (source example: single $35; 3-pack $23/item; 6-pack down to $20/item with $89 saved).
Make the largest tier visually heavier but don't default to it; the source argues the biggest option feels too aggressive for most buyers.
Point all ad creative at the pre-selected tier so traffic and AOV intent match.
caveats: The source's example is True Classic, a brand whose result (reported $500M+) is not a benchmark for other stores.
Auto-selecting a larger quantity can increase returns and exchanges in fit-sensitive categories.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Bundle the same product, not a mixed assortment
cards.summary: Same-SKU bundles (more units, different flavor or color) outperform cross-category assortments because buyers don't want to be forced into items they don't want.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to bundle for a supplement, consumable, or multi-variant product line.
steps: Build bundles around one hero product with quantity, flavor, or color variations.

Avoid bundles that force the customer to take a product they wouldn't buy on its own; the source says mixed cross-category bundles typically underperform because the buyer only wants one or two of the items.
Set the bundle price so the per-item cost steps down visibly across tiers.
Display the bundle as the default purchase path and keep single units available as the anchor.
Track bundle AOV and return rate, not just conversion.
caveats: The source's caution against mixed bundles is his observation, not a tested rule; some categories have genuine routine-based cross-sell (e.g., a full meal kit).
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Frame bundles as 'free' rather than percent off
cards.summary: 'Buy 2 get 1 free' beats the mathematically equivalent '33% off 3' because free outperforms a percentage in the customer's mind.
cards.use_when: Choosing the copy and framing for a multi-unit bundle offer.
steps: Convert your percentage bundle discount into a free-item framing when the quantities allow it.
Use 'buy 2 get 1 free' or 'buy 3 get 2 free' rather than '33% off' or '40% off'.
Keep the same total price as the percent version so the margin impact is unchanged and only the framing differs.
Show the free item's value next to the paid items so the stack is legible.
Always test the two framings directly on the same traffic; the source says 'free always works better' based on their tests.
caveats: The claim that free always beats percent off is a presenter generalization from his company's testing, not a universal rule.
Check that the free-item framing doesn't conflict with your site-wide discount rules or stack into an unintended deeper discount.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Anchor free gift by consumption value
cards.summary: Free gift offers convert, but the source's data shows $25 in store credit beat a generic free gift by roughly 3x on opt-ins and placed-order rate.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a free gift and a cash-equivalent first-order offer in a pop-up or welcome offer.
steps: Don't assume 'free gift' is the strongest offer just because it's been running for years; the source's client had run a free gift offer unchanged for years.
Price the gift's perceived value against a cash-equivalent option at the same cost to you.
Test at minimum: free gift, percent off, dollar off, mystery discount, cash back/store credit, and a bundle.
For an AOV around $250-300, a $25 offer reads at roughly 10%; in the source's test, '$25 in credit' far outperformed both a free gift and 10% off.
Compare on gross profit, not revenue, since gift COGS differs from discount cost.
caveats: The 3x opt-in and 10.7% vs 3.3% placed-order rates are one eight-figure client's test results, not a benchmark.
Store credit only works if you can predict redemption and breakage; otherwise it's a future liability.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Dollar-off vs percent-off by AOV threshold
cards.summary: Above roughly $100 AOV, dollar-off reads bigger; below $100, percent-off reads bigger.
cards.use_when: Writing the headline for a pop-up, first-order offer, or site-wide discount.
steps: Calculate your current AOV.
If AOV is above $100, lead with the dollar amount (e.g., '$25 off' over '10% off' when 10% is $25).
If AOV is below $100, lead with the percentage (e.g., '20% off' rather than '$5 off' at a $50 AOV), because 20 reads larger than 5.
Keep the actual giveaway the same and only change the framing; this isolates the psychology from the economics.
If you're a high-AOV brand currently advertising a percent off, test converting it to the equivalent dollar figure first — the source calls this a frequent, high-leverage switch.
caveats: The $100 AOV threshold and the framing effects are the source's heuristics, not a rigorous benchmark; they are pre-rounded and should be validated on your own traffic.
Very high AOVs can make dollar framing feel like a trivial amount, so retest as price scales.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Stack site-wide offers into one advertised first-order value
cards.summary: Combine your evergreen site discount with the welcome code and advertise the aggregate, so the headline reads as one large dollar figure.
cards.use_when: Writing the pop-up and welcome-flow messaging for a store that already runs a permanent site or subscription discount.
steps: Audit every live discount on your site, including subscription savings, bundle savings, and evergreen promos.
Convert each into the equivalent dollar value at your AOV.
Sum them and advertise the total: the source's example is a 15% site offer plus a 10% welcome code framed as '25% off, you've got $35 off'.
If there's an additional stackable layer, advertise the ceiling: 'up to $50 off your first order'.
Check there are no conflicting or mutually exclusive offers before making the aggregate claim, so the promise survives checkout.
caveats: The claim must be accurate at checkout or you'll generate complaints and cancellations; only advertise what actually stacks.
Stacking an evergreen discount with a welcome code permanently deepens your effective first-order discount; verify margin.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Mystery discount framing
cards.summary: A hidden-value framing ('mystery offer') lifts opt-in because curiosity is added on top of the discount itself.
cards.use_when: Writing pop-up copy to increase email/SMS list opt-in rate, especially when you're not willing to increase discount depth.
steps: Take an offer you would already run (percent, dollar, or gift) and wrap it as a mystery or exclusive unlock.
Keep the underlying value fixed so you can measure the framing effect on opt-in cleanly.
In the source's test, the mystery discount variant (actually $25 off) beat an explicit free gift and 10% off on opt-ins and placed-order rate.
Reveal the actual value in the follow-up message so the promise is delivered.
Separate opt-in rate from placed-order rate when reading results; a framing can win one and lose the other.
caveats: Mystery framing is the source's preferred tactic and their test evidence comes from one brand's eight-variant pop-up test.
If the revealed value feels small, the mystery framing can damage trust.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: What not to run as a first-order offer
cards.summary: The source limits first-order offers to dollar off, percent off, free gift/BOGO, and cash back — and warns against giveaways and free guides.
cards.use_when: Shortlisting the first-order and pop-up offer types when building a lead-capture or acquisition campaign.
steps: Keep the shortlist to: dollar off, percent off, free gift (including buy-one-get-one), and cash back.
Avoid giveaways: the source says they produce low-quality leads that don't convert.
Avoid free guides: the source says intent around them is low because people buy from offers and discounts.
Don't just repeat the same evergreen '10% off' pop-up that most brands run; it doesn't differentiate.
Keep one core offer per segment so you're not contradicting yourself across pop-up, site, and ads.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommendation list based on his agency's work; content-led acquisition and community offers can work in other models.
Giveaway and content strategies may suit categories with long consideration cycles where instant discounts convert poorly.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Measure offers on 90-day LTV, not first order alone
cards.summary: An offer that wins the first purchase can hurt repeat rate, so measure opt-in, placed-order, first-order revenue, and 90-day downstream value.
cards.use_when: Reading the results of a pop-up, first-order, or subscription offer test before rolling it out.
steps: Set up four metrics per variant: opt-in rate, placed-order rate, first-order revenue, and 90-day LTV.
Run the variants against equal traffic so the only difference is the offer itself.
Compare on gross profit rather than revenue, since a discount and a gift have different costs.
Look for offers that improve first-order conversion but depress repeat rate, and weigh them against the LTV gain.
Match the offer to the customer's expected repeat window so the LTV window actually captures the second purchase.
caveats: The source's client example (welcome flow going from $33K to $210K in two months and store revenue up ~$400K) is a single case with no control details, not a forecast.
Stop short of attributing store-wide revenue changes purely to the offer test if other changes were live.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Segment measurement by subscriber status
cards.summary: Comparing subscriber vs non-subscriber cohort LTV at six months shows why subscription conversion should be pushed on the first order.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of the first-order offer budget to spend on pushing subscription rather than one-time purchase.
steps: Build cohorts of subscribers and non-subscribers from first-order date.
Measure LTV at a fixed horizon (the source uses six months) rather than lifetime-to-date, so cohorts are comparable.
In the source's data, subscribers were worth about $226 at month six vs about $138 for non-subscribers.
Use the gap to size how much extra value you can afford to give on the first order to convert a buyer to subscription.
Recheck the gap on your own data before copying the numbers.
caveats: The $226 vs $138 figures come from one agency's custom analytics dashboard and one brand context; they are illustrative, not an industry benchmark.
Subscription cohorts self-select for higher intent, so part of the LTV gap may not be caused by the subscription itself.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Everyday offer plus a flash deals page for urgency
cards.summary: Keep bundles as the evergreen core offer and route urgency ads to a separate limited-time page to convert price-sensitive and overstock buyers.
cards.use_when: Planning merchandising and promo calendar for an apparel or accessory store already running an evergreen bundle.
steps: Keep your main bundle offer evergreen and targeted by most ad creative.
Create a separate flash deals page with a countdown to a fixed time (the source cites midnight) and custom deals on overstocked items.
Show claimed-percentage or stock signals (source example: 79% claimed) to reinforce scarcity.
Link back from the flash page to the core bundle so urgency traffic still sees the main offer.
Refresh the deals or the customers will learn the 'flash' isn't real.
caveats: The source explicitly says he does not know whether True Classic actually refreshes its deals daily; the tactic relies on the customer believing the limited window.
Fake scarcity is regulated in some markets and erodes trust when exposed.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx

cards.title: Research competitor pop-up offers for framing variants
cards.summary: Collect live pop-ups from brands across your space to generate framing variants beyond the plain percent-off.
cards.use_when: Building a backlog of pop-up and first-order offer variants to test.
steps: Browse competitor and adjacent-brand sites and capture the pop-up offer: dollar off, percent off, dollar amounts, mystery, store-credit framing.
Note the exact wording, not just the discount, since the framing is the variable being tested.
Include unusual percentage values (15%, 18%, 17.5%) in your test plan as well as round numbers.
Convert the collected offers into test variants for your own pop-up platform.
Prioritize variants that differ structurally — the source argues swapping only the percentage is not offer testing.
caveats: The source names a specific pop-up tool and its inspiration gallery; verify the current feature set before relying on it.
Copying a competitor's offer without matching their AOV, margin, and category can produce misleading tests.
cards.source_name: I Studied Every $100M Ecommerce Offer So You Don't Have To.docx
